اختيار المحرر الأمم المتحدة تدين تصاعد هجمات المسيّرات في السودان 31 أكتوبر 2026 في اختيار المحرر , الأخبار , الحرب بين الجيش السوداني والدعم السريع , السودان , دولي 0 الأمين العام للأمم المتحدة أنطونيو غوتيريش نيويورك 31 أكتوبر 2026 – أدان الأمين العام للأمم المتحدة، أنطونيو غوتيريش، السبت، تصاعد الهجمات بالطائرات المسيّرة في السودان من جانب أطراف الصراع. وعادت، منذ الأسبوع الماضي، موجة استهداف محطات الكهرباء في معظم أنحاء السودان، حيث تعرضت أكثر من 13 محطة لتوزيع الكهرباء في ولايات القضارف والخرطوم والجزيرة والبحر الأحمر، فضلاً عن سنار والنيل الأبيض وجنوب كردفان، لهجمات وأضرار بالغة تسببت في انقطاع التيار الكهربائي عن عدد من المدن. وقال المتحدث باسم الأمين العام، في بيان، إن غوتيريش “يدين تصاعد الهجمات بالطائرات المسيّرة في السودان من قبل أطراف الصراع، والآثار الكارثية لتلك الهجمات على المدنيين”. وأوضح أن الطائرات المسيّرة قتلت مئات المدنيين في أنحاء السودان، وكذلك في أبيي الواقعة بين السودان وجنوب السودان، بينهم نساء وأطفال، بما يمثل انتهاكات للقانون الدولي الإنساني. واستنكر الأمين العام، في البيان، جميع الهجمات الموجهة ضد المدنيين والبنية التحتية المدنية، بما فيها المرافق الصحية. ودعا أطراف الصراع إلى تجنب تعريض المدنيين والبنية التحتية الحيوية للخطر، والاتفاق دون تأخير على وقف الأعمال العدائية، باعتباره خطوة أولى نحو إنهاء هذا الصراع المدمر. وجدد مناشدته العاجلة للأطراف للانخراط بحسن نية في جهود الوساطة. وأفاد البيان بأن الأمم المتحدة تقف على أهبة الاستعداد لدعم أي جهود تهدف إلى دفع الحل السياسي المستدام الذي يعكس تطلعات الشعب السوداني. الكلمات: أزمة الكهرباء الامم المتحدة الانتهاكات الكهرباء قصف مسيرات معارك الجيش والدعم السريع مقالات ذات صلة باسم الخارجية الأوكرانية هيورهي تيخي الخرطوم 31 أكتوبر 2026 – نفى المتحدث باسم وزارة الخارجية الأوكرانية، هيورهي تيخي، السبت اتهامات سودانية بمشاركة خبراء أوكرانيين في مجال الطائرات المسيّرة في السودان، أو اعتقالهم وبحوزتهم أسلحة، وذلك رداً على تصريحات لوزير الخارجية السوداني، محيي الدين سالم. وكان الوزير السوداني تحدث أمس الجمعة لوكالة الأنباء الروسية عن احتجاز ومقتل عدد من المواطنين الأوكرانيين، قال إنهم كانوا يعملون قناصة ومدربين عسكريين إلى جانب قوات الدعم السريع، خلال المعارك الدائرة في السودان. وقال المسؤول الأوكراني في بيان إنه: «لا تتوفر لدى أوكرانيا أي معلومات تؤكد صحة ما ورد في هذه التصريحات، كما لم تتلقَّ من الجانب السوداني أي اتصالات رسمية بهذا الشأن، وحتى الآن، لم تُقدَّم كذلك أي أدلة موثوقة من شأنها إثبات صحة هذه الادعاءات، وإذا كان لدى الجانب السوداني أي وقائع أو معلومات محددة، فإننا نتطلع إلى تلقي إخطار رسمي بهذا الشأن عبر القنوات الدبلوماسية أو غيرها من القنوات المناسبة، بما يتيح الوقوف على ملابسات الأمر». وقال وزير الخارجية السوداني إنه جرى احتجاز عدد من القناصة والمدربين الأوكرانيين، فيما قُتل آخرون خلال المواجهات، مشيراً إلى أن الجيش استولى كذلك على أسلحة كانت بحوزتهم. ونقلت الوكالة الروسية عن سالم قوله إن بعض المواطنين الأوكرانيين كانوا يشاركون في مهام القنص والتدريب العسكري، إلى جانب عناصر تابعة لقوات الدعم السريع بقيادة محمد حمدان دقلو «حميدتي». وأضاف أن مدربين أوكرانيين ساعدوا عناصر الدعم السريع على تشغيل الطائرات المسيّرة، التي قال إنها استُخدمت في تنفيذ هجمات استهدفت مواقع مدنية. ولم يقدم سالم تفاصيل إضافية بشأن عدد الأوكرانيين الذين جرى احتجازهم أو مقتلهم، أو توقيت ومواقع المواجهات التي شاركوا فيها، كما لم يكشف عن طبيعة الأسلحة التي قال إن الجيش استولى عليها. الكلمات: أخبار السودان. أوكرانيا الجيش السوداني الخرطوم طائرات مسيرة قوات الدعم السريع وزارة الخارجية الأوكرانية مقالات ذات صلة (الشعبية): الحكومة السودانية تستغل وقف sudan.content: السودان يطالب المجتمع الدولي بتحمل مسؤولياته تجاه التواطؤ الإثيوبي - سودان تربيون تخطى الى المحتوى من نحن اتصل بنا English السبت , 31 أكتوبر - 2026 سودان تربيون أخبار السودان وتقارير حصرية لحظة بلحظة الرئيسية سياسة الأخبار تقصي الحقائق اقتصاد دولي اقاليم الرأي English سودان تربيون أخبار السودان وتقارير حصرية لحظة بلحظة الرئيسية الأخبار السودان يطالب المجتمع الدولي بتحمل مسؤولياته تجاه التواطؤ الإثيوبي الأخبار السودان يطالب المجتمع الدولي بتحمل مسؤولياته تجاه التواطؤ الإثيوبي 31 أكتوبر 2026 في الأخبار , الحرب بين الجيش السوداني والدعم السريع , السودان 0 وكيل وزارة الخارجية معاوية عثمان خلال تنوير لرؤساء البعثات الدبلوماسية ببورتسوان- السبت 31 أكتوبر 2026 "سونا" بورتسودان 31 أكتوبر 2026- طالبت وزارة الخارجية السودانية، السبت، المجتمع الدولي بتحمل مسؤولياته إزاء فتح إثيوبيا أراضيها لقصف منشآت الكهرباء ومحطات المياه والوقود والمستشفيات بطائرات مسيّرة تنطلق من قاعدة أصوصا. وعادت منذ الأسبوع الماضي موجة استهداف محطات الكهرباء في معظم أنحاء السودان، حيث تعرضت أكثر من 13 محطة لتوزيع الكهرباء في ولايات القضارف والخرطوم والجزيرة والبحر الأحمر فضلاً عن سنار والنيل الأبيض وجنوب كردفان، لهجمات وأضرار بالغة تسببت في انقطاع التيار الكهربائي عن عدد من المدن. وقال وكيل وزارة الخارجية معاوية عثمان، في تنوير لممثلي البعثات الدبلوماسية عقد في بورتسودان اليوم السبت إن “التنوير استهدف وضع المجتمع الدولي، ممثلًا في البعثات الدبلوماسية المعتمدة لدى السودان، أمام مسؤولياته في التصدي لهذا العدوان الغاشم الذي يأتي من دولة إثيوبيا”. وقدم خالد بالتنسيق مع الأجهزة الأمنية المختصة، عرضاً لحطام المسيّرات التي تم إسقاطها. وأشار إلى أن هذه الهجمات، التي تصاعدت وتيرتها خلال الأشهر الأخيرة، استهدفت البنى التحتية والمنشآت الحيوية بالبلاد، خاصة مرافق إنتاج الكهرباء ومحطات المياه والمدارس والمستشفيات ومحطات الوقود. وأوضح أن الاستهداف الذي تباشره إثيوبيا ظلماً وعدواناً على السودان يمثل حرباً بالوكالة وتؤدي أديس أبابا الدور لصالح أطراف أخرى ودول في الإقليم على رأسها الإمارات وتستخدم “المليشيا” في هذا العدوان كذراع في هذه الهجمات. وتابع خالد “قاعدة أصوصا في إثيوبيا باتت قاعدة لتزويد المليشيا بالسلاح والعتاد وتسهيل مرور المقاتلين الأجانب المرتزقة الذين يشاركون في حرب العدوان على السودان، لكن الأخطر هو استخدام الأراضي والقواعد الإثيوبية منطلقاً للطائرات المسيرة”. وذكر معاوية عثمان أن الحكومة تبذل جهودًا لخفض التصعيد ومعالجة الاختلالات القائمة في العلاقات السودانية الإثيوبية عبر مختلف الوسائل الدبلوماسية. وأعلن احتفاظ السودان بحقه الكامل في الرد على أي عدوان، وفقًا لما يكفله القانون الدولي للدول التي تتعرض للاعتداء. وأشار إلى أن السفراء والدبلوماسيين المشاركين في التنوير أكدوا دعم بلدانهم لوحدة السودان وسيادته وسلامة أراضيه، ووقوفهم إلى جانب الشعب السوداني في محنته حتى تتوقف الحرب وتعود الحياة إلى طبيعتها في البلاد. والأربعاء، قدمت وزارة الدفاع، خلال مؤتمر صحفي، نماذج لطائرات مسيّرة أسقطها الجيش، مرفقة ببيانات فنية بشأن مواقع انطلاقها ومساراتها والأهداف التي استهدفتها والأضرار الناجمة عن الهجمات. وأفادت الوزارة بأن تحليل البيانات المستخلصة من المسيّرات، باستخدام برمجيات حديثة، أظهر إحداثيات انطلاق من مواقع داخل الأراضي الإثيوبية، بينها مطار بحر دار، مشيرة إلى أن صور الأقمار الصناعية تمثل دليلًا إضافيًا على ذلك. وقدم السودان في وقت سابق أدلة إلى مجلس الأمن الدولي بشأن تزويد الإمارات قوات الدعم السريع بالأسلحة والعتاد العسكري، تضمنت مسارات وصولها عبر ليبيا وتشاد وإقليم بونتلاند في الصومال. الكلمات: إثيوبيا البنية التحتية التواطؤ الإثيوبي الخارجية السودانية السودان بورتسودان طائرات مسيرة مجلس الأمن مقالات ذات صلة السودان يواصل ترحيل اللاجئين ارتفاع أسعار قطع الغيار وصعوبة الحصول على بعض المكونات الأصلية، لا تستهدف هذه التعديلات إضافة مزايا تقنية فحسب، بل تسعى أيضا إلى إطالة العمر التشغيلي للسيارات وتخفيف أعباء صيانتها. فكيف يمكن تحويل سيارة قديمة إلى مركبة تعمل بالهاتف؟ وهل تستطيع هذه التعديلات منحها بعض وظائف السيارات الحديثة دون التأثير في سلامتها؟ عقل إلكتروني لسيارة قديمة داخل ورشته في أم درمان، يعمل أيمن سليمان عثمان سليمان، المتخصص في كهرباء وإلكترونيات السيارات، على تحديث أنظمة سيارات يعود إنتاج بعضها إلى أعوام 1998 و2000 و2002. ولا تقتصر أعماله على تركيب أنظمة التشغيل عن بُعد، بل تشمل ما يُعرف بين الفنيين بـ"زراعة الحاسوب"، وهي عملية إدخال وحدة تحكم إلكترونية وربطها بأنظمة متوافقة داخل السيارة. ويوضح أيمن للجزيرة نت أن هذه العملية تتيح استخدام أجهزة الفحص الإلكتروني لقراءة بيانات الأعطال في الأنظمة التي يشملها التعديل، بدلا من الاعتماد على الفحص اليدوي وحده. وتختلف طبيعة التحديثات من سيارة إلى أخرى، بحسب تصميمها الأصلي ومدى توافق الأنظمة الجديدة مع مكوناتها الكهربائية والميكانيكية. تركيب نظام تشغيل عن بعد لسيارة موديل 2002 في السودان (الجزيرة) ويشير أيمن إلى أن الهدف هو إيجاد حلول لمشكلات تواجه أصحاب السيارات القديمة، ولا سيما مع ارتفاع تكلفة قطع الغيار وصعوبة الحصول على بعضها. إعلان ويمكن لهذه التعديلات، عندما تُنفذ بصورة صحيحة، أن تختصر الوقت اللازم لتشخيص بعض الأعطال، وتساعد الفنيين في تحديد مواضع الخلل بدقة أكبر. لكن تركيب وحدة تحكم إلكترونية لا يعني بالضرورة إتاحة فحص جميع أنظمة السيارة، إذ تتوقف القدرات التشخيصية على المكونات والحساسات التي جرى توصيلها بالوحدة الجديدة. كم تكلف هذه التعديلات؟ في الورشة نفسها، يعمل المهندس أحمد العركي على تطوير الأنظمة الإلكترونية لسيارات قديمة، عبر تركيب وحدات تحكم وحساسات جديدة وربطها بالمكونات المتوافقة معها. ويقول العركي للجزيرة نت إن تكلفة تركيب الحاسوب الإلكتروني تبلغ نحو مليون ونصف مليون جنيه سوداني (نحو 2500 دولار)، بينما تصل تكلفة إضافة نظام التشغيل عن بُعد إلى نحو 900 ألف جنيه (نحو 1500 دولار). ويرى أن هذه التكاليف قد تكون مقبولة لبعض مالكي السيارات، مقارنة بالمزايا التي توفرها التعديلات، خصوصا فيما يتعلق بتسهيل تشخيص الأعطال وتقليل الاعتماد على بعض وسائل الفحص التقليدية. لكن التكلفة ليست العامل الوحيد الذي يحدد جدوى العملية، إذ ينبغي مراعاة حالة السيارة الأصلية، وتوافر قطع الغيار، ومدى موثوقية المكونات الجديدة، وتكاليف صيانتها مستقبلا. هل يمكن للهاتف أن يحل محل المفتاح؟ من بين التعديلات التي ينفذها الفنيون تركيب أنظمة تتيح تشغيل محرك السيارة عن بُعد باستخدام الهاتف المحمول أو جهاز تحكم إلكتروني. ويوضح العركي أن هذه الأنظمة تعتمد على برمجة إلكترونية وآلية للتحقق من وسيلة التحكم قبل السماح بالتشغيل. ويشير إلى إمكانية استخدام الهاتف وجهاز التحكم معا، وفقا لطبيعة النظام المركب في السيارة. وقد توفر آليات المصادقة الإلكترونية مستوى إضافيا من الحماية ضد التشغيل غير المصرح به، لكن ذلك يعتمد على تصميم النظام وطريقة تركيبه، ولا يعني بالضرورة أنه يوفر حماية كاملة ضد السرقة. كما أن التشغيل عن بُعد يتطلب التأكد من سلامة التوصيلات ووجود وسائل تمنع التشغيل غير المقصود، خصوصا في السيارات التي لم تُصمم أصلا لهذه الوظيفة. ورشة تعديل أنظمة السيارات بأم درمان (الجزيرة) سيارة من عام 2002 تستجيب للهاتف بالنسبة إلى خالد محمد، مالك سيارة كورية الصنع من موديل 2002، لم يكن الانتقال إلى التشغيل بالهاتف مجرد رغبة في مواكبة التكنولوجيا، فقد عانت سيارته مشكلات متكررة عند تشغيل المحرك، إلى جانب إمكانية تشغيلها باستخدام مفاتيح مختلفة، وهو ما أثار تساؤلات بشأن سلامة نظام التشغيل الأصلي. ويقول خالد للجزيرة نت إن هذه المشكلات دفعته إلى البحث عن حل لدى الفنيين، قبل أن يخضع نظام تشغيل السيارة لتعديل يتيح التحكم فيه عبر الهاتف المحمول. وبذلك حصل على وسيلة تشغيل جديدة لسيارته القديمة، دون الحاجة إلى استبدال المركبة بالكامل. وتعكس تجربة خالد توجها لدى بعض مالكي السيارات إلى البحث عن حلول تقنية تتناسب مع إمكاناتهم المادية، خاصة عندما تصبح تكلفة الإصلاح التقليدي أو توفير بعض القطع الأصلية عبئا متزايدا. تحديث ذكي أم مخاطرة تقنية؟ رغم المزايا التي يمكن أن توفرها هذه الحلول، فإن تحديث الأنظمة الإلكترونية في السيارات القديمة ليس عملية خالية من المخاطر. فتركيب وحدات تحكم أو حساسات غير متوافقة، أو إجراء تعديلات غير محكمة على التوصيلات الكهربائية، قد يتسبب في أعطال جديدة أو يؤثر في موثوقية بعض وظائف السيارة. إعلان ولهذا، ترتبط سلامة التعديلات بخبرة الفنيين، واختيار المكونات المناسبة، وإجراء اختبارات كافية بعد التركيب للتأكد من استقرار الأنظمة الجديدة وعدم تعارضها مع وظائف السيارة الأصلية. وبين ارتفاع تكاليف الصيانة والرغبة في الاستفادة من التقنيات الحديثة، تكشف ورش أم درمان عن محاولات محلية لتطوير السيارات القديمة وإطالة عمرها التشغيلي. فقد لا تحتاج السيارة التي مضى على إنتاجها ربع قرن إلى الاستبدال لمجرد افتقارها إلى بعض التجهيزات الحديثة، لكن منحها وظائف إلكترونية جديدة يظل رهنا بتوافق الأنظمة وسلامة تنفيذها، لا بمجرد قدرتها على الاستجابة لضغطة زر على الهاتف. المصدر: الجزيرة aj-logo Published On 31/10/2026 31/10/2026 | آخر تحديث: 19:12 (توقيت مكة) آخر تحديث: 19:12 (توقيت مكة) في محلية أمبرو بولاية شمال دارفور غرب السودان، يهرب سكان قرى أم حراز وأروري نحو الجبال والوديان، بعد أن دخلت قوات الدعم السريع إلى المنطقة، وسيطرت على جميع آبار المياه، ووضعت سياراتها المسلحة على مصادر الشرب الوحيدة. ويقول أحد السكان، فضّل عدم الكشف عن اسمه، للجزيرة نت، إن الأسر تفرّ منذ صباح الجمعة في كل اتجاه، وإنها تترك خلفها الماشية والأسواق والمحلات التجارية، مؤكدا أن مصير مَن بقي في القرى ما يزال مجهولا. قصص مقترحة list of 2 items list 1 of 2 سيارات قديمة بعقول إلكترونية جديدة.. تجربة لافتة في السودان list 2 of 2 تحركات مصرية لاحتواء التوتر بين السودان وكينيا وتشاد end of list ويضيف أن الاتصالات مقطوعة تماما، وأن ما يخشاه الجميع ليس المعارك فقط، بل الوصول إلى الماء الذي سيطرت عليه القوات، وسط أنباء عن نهب واسع للماشية، وحرق للمراكز الصحية، وتخريب لممتلكات المدنيين. إعلان سيطرة وأعلنت قوات الدعم السريع، أمس الجمعة، سيطرتها على مناطق "مزبد وأروري وكامو" الإستراتيجية في ولاية شمال دارفور، عقب معارك قالت إنها خاضتها ضد الجيش السوداني ومجموعات مسلحة متحالفة معه. وقالت في بيان إن قواتها تمكنت من صد هجوم للجيش والحركات المتحالفة معه، ما دفعها إلى الانسحاب بعد تكبدها خسائر في الأرواح والعتاد، مشيرة إلى الاستيلاء على مركبات قتالية وأسلحة وذخائر لا تزال عملية حصرها جارية. وأضافت أن القوات ستواصل عملياتها في مناطق أخرى بالإقليم، مؤكدة التزامها بحماية المدنيين واستعادة الخدمات الأساسية، بما في ذلك المياه والعلاج. عائلات نزحت من قراها على ظهور دواب نحو مخيم طويلة بدارفور فرارا من قوات الدعم السريع (أرشيفية-الصحافة السودانية) أزمة المياه ولكن الناطق الرسمي باسم المقاومة الشعبية، أبو بكر أحمد إمام، يقول في تصريح حصري للجزيرة نت، إن قوات الدعم السريع هاجمت قرى مدنية ليس بها أي وجود عسكري، وقامت بحرق الأسواق وتدمير المرافق الصحية، قبل أن تسيطر على جميع مصادر المياه الحيوية في محلية أمبرو. ويضيف أن القوات سيطرت على حفيرة وادي أمبار، ودونكي سكر، وآبار منطقة أم حراز، وبئر أم مراحيك، وبئر حوش المعروف بـ"دونكي حوش"، إلى جانب آبار منطقة مجور، ووضعت سياراتها المسلحة عليها، ومنعت السكان والرعاة من الوصول إليها. إعلان ويشير إلى أن هذه الآبار كانت المصدر الرئيسي لمياه الشرب للإنسان والحيوان، خصوصا في المجتمعات الرعوية التي تعتمد حياتها واستقرارها على توفر المياه، وأن السيطرة عليها تعني حرمان آلاف المدنيين من حقهم في الماء، واضطرار الرعاة إلى الفرار نحو الجبال بحثا عن مصادر بديلة. قصف المحطات وسبق أن استهدفت طائرات مسيّرة، تابعة لقوات الدعم السريع، عددا من آبار المياه ومحطات الضخ في شمال دارفور خلال الأشهر الماضية، ما أدى إلى خروجها عن الخدمة وتفاقم أزمة المياه. ففي 21 يوليو/تموز 2026، استهدف قصف بمسيّرة موردا للمياه في منطقة "بئر أندور" بمحلية الطينة، ما أسفر عن مقتل 21 مدنيا على الأقل وإصابة 30 آخرين، كانوا يتجمعون حول البئر لجلب الماء. وفي 12 مايو/أيار 2026، قصفت مسيّرة منطقة "بئر عم صالح" في محلية كرنوي، أحد المصادر الرئيسية للمياه في المنطقة، ما أدى إلى تعطيل البئر بالكامل ونفوق عدد من الماشية، بحسب غرفة طوارئ كرنوي. نداء عاجل وفي بيانها الصادر يوم الجمعة، حذّرت المقاومة الشعبية من أن حرمان المواطنين من الوصول إلى مياه الشرب لا يمثل مجرد أزمة خدمية، بل يشكل تهديدا مباشرا للحياة، وينذر بكارثة إنسانية قد تتفاقم إلى العطش والجوع ونفوق الماشية. ودعت أهلها في مناطق دار زغاوة إلى توخي الحيطة والحذر، وناشدت المنظمات الإنسانية التحرك الفوري لتوفير مياه الشرب والمساعدات الضرورية، وطالبت بضمان وصول السكان إلى مصادر المياه دون عوائق، وحماية الآبار التي تعتمد عليها المجتمعات المحلية في البقاء. بيانات النزوح وتشير بيانات المنظمة الدولية للهجرة إلى أن 895 شخصا نزحوا من قرى "قور بورا" و"جكتورا" و"أم حراز" بمحافظة أمبرو يوم 24 أكتوبر/تشرين الأول 2026، وأن غالبية الأسر عبرت الحدود إلى تشاد المجاورة. وتوضح المنظمة أن الوضع في المنطقة "لا يزال متوترا ومتقلبا للغاية"، وأنها تواصل مراقبة التطورات عن كثب، في ظل تقارير عن نهب واسع للماشية والأسواق، وحرق مراكز صحية، وتخريب لممتلكات المدنيين. وفي محلية أمبرو، حيث تتواصل المعارك وتنقطع الاتصالات، ينتظر المدنيون أي خبر عن مصيرهم، بينما تفرّ الأسر نحو الجبال بلا ماء، وتقف سيارات مسلحة على الآبار التي كانت تسقي الناس والماشية. وتبقى الأسئلة: هل سيجد النازحون مأوى آمنا ومياها قبل أن يحصدهم العطش؟ ومتى يعود العالم ليرى ما يجري في "أم حراز" و"أروري" قبل أن يطويهم النسيان؟ المصدر: الجزيرة aj-logo aj-logo aj-logo إعلان من نحن من نحن اعرض المزيد من نحن الأحكام والشروط سياسة الخصوصية سياسة ملفات تعريف القواعد والأراضي الإثيوبية منطلقا لشن هجمات بالمسيّرات على السودان"، وفق وكالة الأنباء السودانية. وأضاف أن هذه الهجمات "تصاعدت خلال الأشهر الأخيرة، واستهدفت البنية التحتية والمنشآت الحيوية، لا سيما مرافق إنتاج الكهرباء ومحطات المياه والمدارس والمستشفيات ومحطات الوقود، وأسفرت عن مقتل وإصابة المئات". وأوضح وكيل وزارة الخارجية أن الاجتماع استهدف وضع المجتمع الدولي، ممثلا في البعثات الدبلوماسية المعتمدة لدى السودان، أمام مسؤولياته في التصدي لما وصفه بـ"العدوان الغاشم" القادم من إثيوبيا. وقال إن الحكومة السودانية "تبذل جهودا لخفض التصعيد ومعالجة الاختلالات في العلاقات السودانية الإثيوبية عبر مختلف الوسائل الدبلوماسية، مع احتفاظ السودان بحقه الكامل في الرد على أي عدوان، وفقا لما يكفله القانون الدولي للدول التي تتعرض للاعتداء". وأشار خالد إلى أن السفراء والدبلوماسيين المشاركين في الاجتماع "أكدوا دعم بلدانهم لوحدة السودان وسيادته وسلامة أراضيه، ووقوفهم إلى جانب الشعب السوداني حتى تتوقف الحرب وتعود الحياة إلى طبيعتها". والأربعاء، اتهم خالد إثيوبيا بمواصلة "عدوانها على السودان"، معتبرا أن سلوكها "بات خطيرا". وتأتي هذه التصريحات عقب هجمات بطائرات مسيّرة استهدفت 10 محطات كهرباء في ولايات الخرطوم (العاصمة) والجزيرة (وسط) وسنار والقضارف (شرق)، منذ الاثنين الماضي. ومنذ أبريل/ نيسان 2023، Photos shared by him on social media show him taking part in military exercises alongside ministers, deputy ministers and heads of government institutions at the Hurso military training centre. The move is unusual in Ethiopia, where senior civilian government officials are rarely seen undergoing military training. Those taking part include Speaker of the House of Federation Muferiat Kamil, Finance Minister Fitsum Assefa and Health Minister Mekdes Daba. It is unclear when the training began or how long it is expected to last. In his post, the prime minister, who is known as Abiy, said Ethiopia's ambition to achieve universal prosperity required its leadership to be physically fit, morally strong and intellectually capable. He said military institutions offered valuable lessons in discipline, patriotism, teamwork, accountability and leadership. "Soldiers have targets while civilians have goals. The objective of both is victory," he said, adding that combining military and civilian disciplines would help create a generation capable of achieving both. Abiy argued that military training could help develop leaders with a strong sense of purpose, responsibility and the ability to work together towards common objectives. The training comes as Ethiopia faces multiple security challenges, including continued fighting in parts of the northern Tigray region, conflict in Amhara and insecurity in Oromia. It also takes place amid heightened tensions with neighbouring Eritrea, with concerns over the possibility of renewed conflict between the two countries. Abiy has previously emphasised military preparedness and national development as central to his government's ambitions. Opposition Parties, UN Agencies Sound Alarm Over Security Incidents, Civilian Safety in Ethiopia 3 minute read By Abraham Tekle October 31, 2026 Share Facebook X WhatsApp Linkedin Email Telegram Copy URL UN agencies report tens of thousands fled to Kenya Opposition political parties and United Nations agencies have voiced mounting concern over civilian casualties, security incidents, and displacement across parts of Ethiopia, urging immediate measures to protect citizens, investigate reported violations, and ensure accountability amid ongoing regional violence. The Ethiopian Citizens for Social Justice (EZEMA), in a statement issued on October 27, expressed concern that the government has fallen short of its primary obligation to ensure public safety. EZEMA also criticized public media outlets, including the Ethiopian Broadcasting Corporation (EBC), for omitting reports of civilian casualties following incidents in the Arsi Zone of the Oromia Region earlier in the month. Detailing multiple security challenges, the party noted that violence in Arsi, alongside recurring inter-communal clashes in the past months in Gambella and Moyale, has led to loss of life, displacement, and property damage. EZEMA called on federal authorities to take proactive steps to prevent further escalations, transparently investigate institutional shortcomings, and hold responsible parties accountable. Furthermore, the party urged human rights organizations to independently examine the incidents and called for greater public media scrutiny regarding the government’s crisis response. The party appealed to federal and regional authorities to thoroughly investigate the violations, safeguard civilians, and prosecute perpetrators regardless of their official standing or political affiliation. It also encouraged international organizations, diplomatic missions, and human rights monitors to closely follow the situation, cautioning that it is prepared to organize peaceful public demonstrations under the slogan ‘Beka!’ (Enough!) if its demands for security and accountability remains unmet. Echoing these concerns, the Ethiopian People’s Revolutionary Party (EPRP) issued a statement condemning killings, abductions, and forced displacements in the Arsi Zone, specifically highlighting Shirka and Chole districts. Citing local information, the party reported multiple deaths, injuries, and the alleged abduction of approximately 50 individuals from their homes. The EPRP advocated for an independent international investigation, the safe release of abducted persons, humanitarian assistance for displaced populations, and legal action against those culpable. These developments align with findings from the Ethiopian Human Rights Council (EHRCO), which documented a pattern of killings, injuries, abductions, and displacement across Oromia, Amhara, Gambella, and Benishangul-Gumuz in its annual human rights report covering June 2025 to June 2026. The council reiterated calls for regional and federal authorities to prioritize civilian protection and comprehensive investigations. Tsimdo refers to armed forces who claims to forge alliance against the government. Hailu expressed deep regret over the loss of lives and material damage resulting from the unrest. Concurrently, reports of active conflict and civilian casualties have emerged from the Amhara and Tigray regions. International media reported that drone strikes hit the Jari No. 2 displacement camp in the South Wollo Zone of the Amhara Region, resulting in a reported death toll including children—alongside numerous injuries requiring hospitalization. In the Tigray Region of Rama town, local residents reported a separate strike affecting a truck transporting sorghum, causing casualties among individuals gathered at the scene. Additional reports from October detailed airstrikes and drone activity in Adwa, Shire, and Sheraro, resulting in civilian deaths and damage to local infrastructure. The impact of the ongoing security challenges has also spilled across international borders. According to the UN Refugee Agency (UNHCR), clashes near the Ethiopian-Kenyan border have prompted thousands to cross into Kenya via Moyale since October 22. Local authorities estimate that up to 50,000 individuals have crossed, with registration and verification efforts ongoing. Many of those fleeing are women and children, finding temporary shelter in local schools, churches, or with host communities. In response, the UNHCR, alongside the International Organization for Migration (IOM), UNICEF, and the World Food Programme, has launched an appeal for USD8.9 million to provide essential humanitarian assistance to up to 50,000 displaced individuals over a three-month period. The IOM indicated that humanitarian partners are actively preparing for further arrivals. Addressing the broader climate of conflict, UN Secretary-General António Guterres emphasized in a public statement that adherence to international law, addressing root causes, and pursuing political settlements remain the only viable pathways to sustainable peace. “Let’s summon the political will to silence the guns, stop the killing, and build a world where peace for all prevails,” he stated. From the Cradle of the Nile: Ethiopia’s Sea-Access Ambitions Take Center Stage at Tana 10 minute read By Ashenafi Endale October 31, 2026 Share Facebook X WhatsApp Linkedin Email Telegram Copy URL Sitting on the southern shores of Lake Tana—the mystical, sprawling cradle of the Blue Nile—Bahir Dar offers a striking, almost poetic metaphor for the turbulence currently gripping the Horn of Africa and the wider continent. The Nile has long flowed as the lifeblood of East and North African hydropolitics, binding nations together in an inescapable web of shared geography, competing ambitions, and intense historical rivalry. It was precisely within this metaphorical watershed that policymakers, regional leaders, senior military commanders, and prominent researchers gathered for the 12th Edition of the Tana High-Level Forum on Security in Africa. Returning after a hiatus forced by escalating regional conflicts, the 2026 summit convened under the sharp, pragmatic theme dubbed ‘Pathways to Peace in Africa: Economic Sovereignty and Geopolitical Transformation.’ Yet, while official panel sessions wrestled with the high-minded mechanics of continental trade integration, digital imperialism, monetary frameworks, and macroeconomic governance, the dominant pulse of the conference floor belonged to an unyielding national imperative. Ethiopia’s bold, unapologetic push for reliable, sovereign sea access, set against a backdrop of deep continental fragmentation, the ravages of conflict economies in Sudan and the Sahel, and the urgent demand for structural self-reliance. The deep symbolism of the host city itself exerts its own weigh on the debates that unfolded in Bahirdar. Lake Tana is not merely a geographical landmark; it is the origin point of the Blue Nile, a river that sustains millions downstream while fueling a century-old geopolitical contest over water security, sovereignty, and regional hegemony. In this light, hosting a premier security summit dedicated to economic sovereignty and geopolitical transformation on the very banks of the Nile is deeply profound. From The Reporter Magazine Drought Emergency or Seasonal Deficit ? Published on 2026-09-02 By The Reporter Magazine What the Old Developmental State Got Wrong Published on 2026-10-02 By Samson Berhane 25-Year Sentences & Retroactive Laws: Controversial Draft Law Sparks Fears of Growing Authoritarianism in Tigray Published on 2026-06-21 By Yared Nigussie Red Sea Rivalries: What a Shifting Geopolitical Landscape Means for Ethiopia and The Horn Published on 2026-08-31 By Yared Nigussie East Africa’s enduring hydropolitical tension is mirrored by Ethiopia’s modern strategic dilemma. A nation of over 130 million people, locked behind borders drawn by historical compromises, is seeking a permanent economic outlet to the world. This geographic vulnerability forms the crucible in which Ethiopia’s current foreign policy is forged. When PM Abiy Ahmed took the podium to open the summit, he did not shy away from the persisting core structural realities. Urging African states to shape rather than merely adapt to global power shifts, Abiy placed sovereignty at the center of the continental dialogue, declaring that Africa must stop being a passive recipient of external prescriptions and instead author its own destiny. “By combining its capacities and developing solutions suited to its own realities, Africa can strengthen its role in shaping the global order and securing a better future for generations to come,” Abiy noted, stressing that homegrown solutions are non-negotiable for lasting stability. From The Reporter Magazine From Unwilling Investors to Bidding Wars: Ethiopia’s T-Bill Market Turns on Its Head Published on 2026-09-03 By Mahlet Mehdi Washington Has Sent a Sufficient Signal to PM Abiy on Military Operations: Ex-CIA Analyst Published on 2026-09-28 By Bewket Abebe Behind Ethiopia’s Stalled Iron Ore Mining Published on 2026-08-29 By Bewket Abebe Cities as Engines of Growth and Nation-Building: Reframing Urbanization Discourses in Sub-Saharan Africa (SSA) Published on 2026-09-14 By Mussie Delelegn Arega (PhD) Crucially, anchoring this push for strategic autonomy, Ethiopian leadership articulated the core national doctrine that secure, unfettered access to the sea is an existential necessity for a growing population of over 130 million, rather than a negotiable diplomatic luxury or a casual geopolitical preference. That message was echoed with striking, unvarnished directness by Ethiopia’s top security and defense leadership. Redwan Hussein, director general of Information Network Security Administration (INSA) and Field Marshal Berhanu Jula, Chief of Staff of Ethiopian National Defense Force (ENDF), underscored during the deliberations that Ethiopia’s national interest in maritime access, framing it not as an aggressive encroachment on neighbors, but as a vital economic lifeline required to prevent structural strangulation and ensure long-term regional stability. However, behind closed doors, in the academic corridors, and among international policy observers, this rhetoric met with analytical scrutiny. Regional and international scholars immediately posed the hard, skeptical question of whether Ethiopian officials are simply staking out a long-term bargaining position to secure alternative port arrangements in a volatile neighborhood, or if there is a tangible, realistic, and peaceful roadmap on the table. Critics note that while the rallying national agenda of maritime rights galvanizes domestic political consensus, navigating the hostile geopolitical realignments of the Red Sea basin demands far more than political will. With the Horn of Africa caught in a web of shifting alliances—marked by friction between Asmara, Cairo, Port Sudan, and Mogadishu, alongside mounting Middle Eastern proxy interventions—analysts warn that uncalibrated maritime ambitions risk inflaming already volatile fault lines unless backed by transparent, cooperative diplomatic frameworks. Presenters and researchers also emphasized that maritime access cannot be separated from the broader architecture of regional trust, arguing that any sustainable framework must reconcile Ethiopia’s legitimate economic needs with the sovereignty and security concerns of neighboring littoral states. The urgency of Ethiopia’s national posture played out against the grim, comprehensive diagnosis detailed in the Tana Secretariat’s official State of Peace and Security in Africa Report, which was presented to the delegates by Tana Board Chairperson and former Ghanaian President John Dramani Mahama. The report paints a sobering, data-driven picture of a continent grappling with the dangerous regionalization of violence, the institutionalization of conflict economies, and the erosion of multilateral mediation. Nowhere was this regional contagion more pronounced than in the ongoing catastrophe in Sudan. According to the report’s two-phase analysis covering January 2025 to June 2026, the war underwent a qualitative shift following RSF’s capture of El Fasher, cementing the country’s complete territorial and political fragmentation, with the RSF controlling western gold corridors and the Sudanese Armed Forces holding Khartoum and eastern red sea routes. Panelists detailed how the conflict is sustained by the direct and indirect commodification of violence, where illicit gold trade funnels upwards of USD400 million annually into war chests, financing recruitment, weaponry, and the proliferating use of drones. This internal war has inevitably spilled across borders, drawing in Chad, South Sudan, Egypt, Ethiopia, and proximate Gulf powers, transforming the wider region into a theater of competing middle-power rivalries. Mahama himself underscored the human cost of these dynamics, warning the assembly that Africa cannot achieve economic sovereignty while entire populations are displaced and state institutions collapse under the weight of resource-driven civil wars. The summit also turned a critical eye toward the intractable crises in the eastern DRC, where despite diplomatic milestones like the Declaration of Principles and the Washington Accord, fighting between M23 and government forces has deepened humanitarian tragedies, with rare earth mineral extraction fueling regional logistics networks. In Somalia, the complex security transition from ATMIS to AUSSOM in Somalia, combined with domestic friction over constitutional reform and resource distribution, continues to provide fertile ground for Al-Shabaab’s insurgency, resonating across the wider Red Sea space. Further south, the conflict in Cabo Delgado, Mozambique, has mutated into an elusive rural insurgency where local perceptions of economic exclusion around liquefied natural gas projects threaten to re-ignite communal grievances. Accounting for roughly 55 percent of all conflict-related fatalities on the continent, the Sahel remains Africa’s most volatile security theater, where the withdrawal of Mali, Burkina Faso, and Niger from ECOWAS to form the Alliance of Sahel States has dismantled regional coordination, creating security vacuums exploited by jihadist groups. Compounding this instability is a profound technological shift in warfare: the proliferation of commercial and military drones by state and non-state actors across at least nine African countries for reconnaissance, explosive attacks, and online propaganda, cheapening the cost of conflict while exponentially increasing civilian casualties. Moving beyond traditional military paradigms, the 2026 Tana Forum dedicated substantial deliberation to the structural economic traps that underpin continental instability, with panelists and working papers arguing forcefully that security cannot be achieved in an economic vacuum. Delegates dissected the enduring legacy of extractive enclave economies, where African nations export critical raw materials while capturing virtually none of the value-addition, processing revenues, or industrial capabilities. This structural dependency, compounded by heavy debt burdens, unfavorable global trade terms, and reliance on third-party currencies for trade settlement, drains foreign reserves and starves domestic productive sectors of credit. Presenters called for a holistic redefinition of resource sovereignty, arguing that true sovereignty requires exercising total agency across the entire financial and industrial circuit, from local mineral processing and transparent resource-backed lending to domestic invoicing and strengthening intra-African trade channels anchored by the African Continental Free Trade Area. Parallel sessions on the continent’s severe energy deficit, where roughly 600 million Africans still lack reliable electricity, emphasized that regional power integration and transboundary energy pools are indispensable prerequisites for industrialization and sustainable peace. In an era where geopolitical competition has migrated into cyberspace, the forum issued sharp warnings regarding Africa’s digital vulnerability, stressing that digitalization cannot be treated merely as a matter of basic connectivity or technological modernization. When data ecosystems, cloud systems, algorithms, and artificial intelligence are owned and governed externally, African economies risk falling into a modern trap of digital imperialism, prompting experts to demand that African institutions build domestic capabilities in data governance, computing infrastructure, algorithmic transparency, and local software authorship to foster genuine economic independence. Another core pillar of the summit was the complex intersection between regional integration, informal markets, and transnational illicit economies. While the African Union champions regional integration as a vital economic and peace-building tool, the forum acknowledged that formal trade policies alone cannot overcome the realities on the ground, given that a massive share of Africa’s employment and economic activity occurs within the informal sector, functioning as a vital form of bottom-up integration that sustains vulnerable populations across porous borders. However, a critical analytical distinction was drawn between benign informality and destructive illicit economies, noting that while informal cross-border trade provides essential livelihoods, transnational illicit networks, including arms trafficking, environmental plunder, and large-scale trade mis-invoicing by corporate actors, actively fund armed insurgencies and undermine state authority. Empirical papers presented at the forum demonstrated that illicit financial flows are highly adaptive, persisting across fiscal years through entrenched institutional networks, leading delegates to conclude that security and economic integration must go hand in hand, replacing enforcement-only crackdowns with gradual formalization, stronger customs oversight, and the dismantling of high-level illicit financial circuits. As the three-day summit drew to its conclusion, delegates confronted the ultimate, recurring question that haunts high-level diplomatic convenings regarding whether the recommendations emerging from the Tana Forum are legally binding policy mandates or merely an elite agenda-setting platform. The institutional reality is clear. The Tana Forum possesses no direct enforcement mechanism, and its true power lies in its unique, informal character modeled after the traditional African baobab tree, serving as a candid intellectual incubator where sitting leaders, former heads of state, civil society actors, and researchers can speak frankly outside rigid diplomatic protocols. Yet, as Tana Board Chairperson and former Ghanaian President John Dramani Mahama bluntly warned in his powerful closing address, the era of endless dialogue must yield to concrete implementation if the forum is to retain its credibility, asserting that it is good to talk and dialogue, but far better to act. Concluding the summit with a direct appeal for continental transformation, Mahama urged leaders “Let us return to Bahirdar next year and say that the tide is turning for Africa, that our conflicts are ending, and opportunities are being created for all our people.” To transform continental agency from a political slogan into tangible reality, the forum’s final recommendations mapped out a rigorous path forward, including granting Regional Economic Communities predictable and multi-year institutional funding rather than leaving them at the mercy of short-term donor whims when deploying peace support operations. Presenters also emphasized the necessity of institutionalizing public accountability by establishing transparent tracking mechanisms, such as public publication of treaty-ratification statuses, independent performance assessments of early-warning systems, and granting parliaments and media access to continental security data to ensure governments honor their commitments. Furthermore, researchers and panelists stressed the urgency of bridging the dangerous gap between detecting security risks and mobilizing rapid institutional responses before local disputes cascade into full-scale regional wars, while ensuring that formal peace agreements integrate economic restructuring, equitable resource-sharing, and local benefit thresholds to make peace structurally more profitable than war for conflict protagonists. Backdropped by the eternal, life-giving flow of the Blue Nile in Bahirdar, the 12th Tana High-Level Forum on Security in Africa delivered a stark, uncompromising message. Whether confronting Ethiopia’s bold geopolitical push for maritime access, managing the devastating resource-driven fragmentation of Sudan and the Sahel, or building robust economic and digital sovereignty, Africa’s path to sustainable peace requires moving past rhetorical posturing into disciplined, unified action. The intellectual framework has been laid bare by scholars, leaders, and security chiefs alike, and whether African governance structures possess the political discipline and institutional courage to translate these recommendations into hard policy remains the ultimate, defining test for the continent’s future. Drawing on the Forum recommendations, mainstreaming and working on the implementation part; takes African governments, international partners, regional and continental organizations renewing their commitments, actionable plans. The summit, themed "Pathways to Peace in Africa: Economic Sovereignty and Geopolitical Transformation," brought together policymakers and military leaders to discuss pressing regional issues. Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed emphasized the necessity of maritime access for Ethiopia's over 130 million citizens, framing it as essential for economic stability rather than a diplomatic luxury. However, analysts raised concerns about the feasibility of these ambitions amid regional tensions and the complex geopolitical landscape of the Red Sea. The forum also addressed broader security challenges in Africa, including the ongoing conflicts in Sudan and the DRC, highlighting the need for economic sovereignty to achieve lasting peace. The discussions underscored the interconnectedness of security and economic stability across the continent. (157 words)

ethiopia.content: The Red Sea Chokehold: Why Maritime Access Is an Existential Question for Ethiopia – HORN REVIEW Home About Us Team Research and Analysis Horn Geopolitics Global Politics Ethiopia and the World Publications News Reports and Articles Horn Review Journal Articles Horn Review Magazine Report Amharic Publications Amharic News Reports and Articles Amharic Research and Analysis Amharic Ethiopia and the World Amharic Global Politics Amharic Horn Geopolitics Amharic Horn Review Journal Articles Amharic horn review magazine Amharic Report News and Events Contact Us Search Home About Us Team Research and Analysis Horn Geopolitics Global Politics Ethiopia and the World Publications News Reports and Articles Horn Review Journal Articles Horn Review Magazine Report Amharic Publications Amharic News Reports and Articles Amharic Research and Analysis Amharic Ethiopia and the World Amharic Global Politics Amharic Horn Geopolitics Amharic Horn Review Journal Articles Amharic horn review magazine Amharic Report News and Events Contact Us 2026-10-31 The Red Sea Chokehold: Why Maritime Access Is an Existential Question for Ethiopia 0 Comments For a landlocked nation, maritime access is rarely a matter of simple commerce; it is an existential variable that dictates economic survival, sovereign autonomy, and strategic viability. When a country’s geographic bottleneck is policed by a deeply militarized dictator with no clear economic vision, the resulting friction transcends ordinary bilateral disputes, elevating infrastructure into a primary casus belli. No regional dynamic illustrates this geopolitical chokehold more acutely than the volatile relationship between Ethiopia and Eritrea. For decades, international observers have viewed Ethiopia’s quest for a seaport through a purely commercial lens, equating it as a matter of trade balances, shipping tariffs, and economic optimization. But as the Red Sea rapidly transforms into one of the most volatile, hyper-militarized maritime corridors on the planet, this perspective is dangerously obsolete. For Ethiopia, a nation of over 130 million people, permanent and reliable access to the sea is no longer just an economic aspiration. It is an existential imperative for national security and survival. This assertion makes sense if viewed critically beyond a shallow attempt to reduce the looming danger to a simple expansionist ambition. One must always reconsider the facts on the ground while analyzing the conundrum in the Horn of Africa. Ethiopia, a country that is only 60 kms from the Red sea, is the most populous landlocked country in the world, whose significant portion of the population is youth and in active pursuit of job opportunities. According to recent IMF reports, the country is also home to the fastest growing economy in the entire sub-Saharan Africa. This is not merely a statistical trivia point framed for political purpose; rather it is a profound strategic vulnerability. Every piece of medicine, fuel, and technology that enters the country, and every single product exported to sustain its economy, depends entirely on the political whims and stability of its coastal neighbors. Currently, Ethiopia relies on Djibouti for roughly 95% of its trade, paying upwards between $1.5 to $2 billion annually in port fees. This single door dependency is an economic chokehold. No sovereign state can safely anchor its future on a single corridor that is vulnerable to external influences. For countries like Ethiopia, the highly volatile security situation in its surrounding doubles down the impact, without mentioning the challenges associated with the growing number of military bases in the region. Should political instability or hostile foreign influence freeze the docks of Djibouti, the Ethiopian economy would collapse triggering an internal humanitarian catastrophe of unprecedented scale. This is what makes Ethiopia’s concern undeniably legitimate and fuels its determination to address what it perceives as an existential threat through any means available. Just as a drowning person instinctively tries every possible option to stay afloat. A nation of 130 million people cannot be trapped in a geographic cage at the mercy of volatile, highly militarized autocratic coastal regime. A stable, secure Horn of Africa is impossible if its largest engine of population and economic powerhouse is kept in a state of permanent anxiety and artificial suffocation. Securing a permanent and dependable commercial and naval gateway to the Red Sea is not an empire building ambition or a luxury. For Ethiopia, it is becoming a simple, legitimate right to breath and it is the only way to bring peace and security in the entire Horn. Encirclement, Exclusion, and Ethiopia’s Security Imperative The urgency underpinning Ethiopia’s vulnerability has been sharply accelerated by the growing securitization of the Red Sea. What was once an open global trade route has become an arena for geopolitical chess, dominated by state coalitions and non-state actors from near and afar. Global and regional powers increasingly framing the vital corridor as a critical national security priority rather than just a commercial shipping lane. Driven by the need to safeguard chokepoints like the Bab el Mandab Strait from asymmetric threats, piracy, and regional conflicts, world powers have rapidly expanded their footprint through a dense concentration of military bases along the coastline. Djibouti has become the primary epicenter of this militarization, uniquely hosting overlapping naval facilities for both the United States (Camp Lemonnier) and China, alongside presence from France and Japan. Concurrently, nations like Russia have sought access, while regional actors such as Saudi Arabia, the UAE, Turkye, and Israel are all vying for influence via port logistics and security pacts along the broader Horn of Africa. While these external militaries provide short-term protection for international shipping, their crowding presence has ultimately transformed the Red Sea into a complex arena of overlapping geopolitical rivalries and proxy vulnerabilities, weakening the prospects for a self-sustaining regional security framework and brutally doubling down on Ethiopia’s unique vulnerability. As if these threats are not enough, Ethiopia is alarmed by a recent development of an architectural web of alliances orchestrated explicitly to isolate it from its own geographic backyard. The creation of the El Alamein Joint Declaration by Egypt, Eritrea, and Somalia is not as a routine diplomatic pact, but a deliberate strategy of encirclement. By codifying that Red Sea governance belongs exclusively to coastal states, regional adversaries seek to permanently deny landlocked Ethiopia a seat at the table. Proofing that the danger felt by Ethiopia is eminent beyond perception and this could potentially leave the country to consider every option to break the chokehold before it is too late. The action Ethiopia should take would be determined based on the scale and level of threats the country is faced with, as the end justifies the means. This encirclement is amplified by Egypt’s aggressive forward deployment rhetoric in the region. Driven by tensions over the Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam (GERD), Cairo is trying to weaponize Ethiopia’s landlocked status by forming tight military and logistical alliances with Eritrea and other states bordering Ethiopia. From the Ethiopian perspective, it is quite clear. Hostile foreign militaries are aspiring to setting up base camps right on its borders, holding the keys to the very maritime gates that feed the Ethiopian population. This is a recuring dangerous move. Previously, when multinational coalitions form to protect Red Sea shipping lines from asymmetric threats like piracy and militant groups, Ethiopia is routinely excluded. Addis Ababa is being forced to watch from the sidelines while its primary economic lifeblood is policed by an alliance sympathetic to its rivals. It is profoundly naïve to expect Ethiopia to remain passive while such a perilous scheme is being orchestrated to threaten the lives of its entire population and its very survival. This reality underscores Ethiopia’s existential need to secure a reliable maritime corridor through which it can establish dependable port services and maintain a sovereign naval capability. Such a capability is essential to safeguard its national interests, protect its flag-bearing vessels, and guarantee its unhindered right to innocent passage under international law. Ethiopia has consistently expressed its preference for cooperation and has repeatedly advanced frameworks centered on mutual economic integration, shared prosperity, and regional interdependence. However, while Ethiopia remains committed to peaceful collaboration, coastal states, particularly Eritrea, should recognize that legal technicalities or strategies aimed at regional containment cannot serve as sustainable solutions to a matter that directly concerns the livelihood, security, and future of such burgeoning population. When the survival and long-term interests of the entire nation is at stake, it is unrealistic to expect Ethiopia to remain passive. It will undoubtedly pursue all the necessary strategic measures to secure its legitimate access to the Red Sea and protect its vital national interests. In doing so, it will ensure that its sovereignty, security, and economic future are safeguarded both on land and at sea. In conclusion, Ethiopia’s demand for access to the sea must be understood by its neighbouring countries as a legitimate strategic and economic and security concerns that deserves serious, constructive, and peaceful consideration. Why would Ethiopia’s quest to establish a military base along the Red Sea coast be considered unacceptable when countries from far beyond the region already maintain military bases and enjoy strategic access to the same coastline? Is it just to deny a neighbouring country with vital security and economic interests in the region an opportunity to negotiate such access, while external powers are permitted to establish a military presence there? The issue should not be approached through double standards or geopolitical rivalries, but through constructive dialogue, mutual respect, and negotiated arrangements that uphold the sovereignty of coastal states while addressing Ethiopia’s legitimate interests. IGAD and the African Union must urgently take their leadership responsibilities by facilitating inclusive regional dialogue and developing a practical framework that addresses Ethiopia’s legitimate aspirations while safeguarding the legitimate interests of neighbouring states. External actors outside the Horn of Africa should be discouraged from pursuing their agendas by fostering hostility and division, rather than promoting cooperation, dialogue, and regional stability. The international community, including the United Nations and other influential partners, should also intensify diplomatic engagement and support a negotiated settlement before the situation deteriorates into a dangerous confrontation with far reaching consequences for the Horn of Africa and beyond. The time to act is now: through timely diplomacy, mutual understanding, and political courage, regional leaders and international stakeholders can transform a potential source of conflict into an opportunity for cooperation, shared prosperity, and lasting peace. Failure to act decisively today risks allowing tensions to spiral into a devastating conflict that the region and the wider world can ill afford. The port of Assab and the risk of an Ethiopia-Eritrea war Amgad Fareid Eltayeb last update on 30 Oct 2026 The dispute between Ethiopia and Eritrea over the Red Sea port of Assab now extends well beyond that of a maritime facility or outlet for international trade. It reflects a structural contradiction between two states with a shared history but divided on issues like sovereignty, security, borders, and the state itself. For Ethiopia, Assab embodies its historical loss of direct access to the sea. This is a growing strategic concern, with the country’s population and economy both having expanded. For Eritrea, the port is a key and inseparable part of its sovereignty, won through a long war of independence. Thus, the port mixes economic interests with domestic power struggles, regional alliances, and foreign intervention, particularly in a region already afflicted by weak state institutions and protracted armed conflicts. The modern roots of the crisis lie in Italian colonial expansion in the 19th century. Italian control of Assab began in 1869 through the Rubattino shipping company, which acquired the right to administer the port from local authorities. Administration passed to the Italian state in 1882, and Assab subsequently became part of Italian Eritrea, formally established as a colony in 1890. With the opening of the Suez Canal in 1869, this was a time of intensifying European competition for ports and trade routes through the Red Sea. Italy lost control of East Africa in 1941, when Assab and the rest of Eritrea came under British occupation and administration. Following the Second World War, Eritrea’s future administration was debated. On 2 December 1950, the UN General Assembly adopted Resolution 390, recommending the establishment of a federation between Eritrea and Ethiopia. The arrangement came into effect in 1952. It recognised Ethiopia’s legitimate need for access to the sea, and granted autonomy to Eritrea (with its own legislative, executive and judicial institutions responsible for internal affairs) within a federation under the sovereignty of the Ethiopian Crown. The resolution did not grant Ethiopia permanent ownership of Assab as a separate sovereign possession, but it went beyond a commercial agreement between two independent states by establishing a federation with sovereign authority at the federal level, defined powers, and Eritrean autonomy. These legal distinctions remain essential to assessing the competing claims surrounding Assab today. Emperor Haile Selassie gradually undermined Eritrea’s autonomous institutions before abolishing the federal system and fully annexing the territory in 1962. A year earlier, Eritrea’s armed struggle for independence had already begun. The Ethiopian Empire fell in the revolution of 1974, and the military regime of Mengistu Haile Mariam reasserted centralised control through force. Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF) fighters arrive after eight hours of walking in Mekele, the capital of the Tigray region, Ethiopia, on 29 June 2021. Alliances and interests Opposition to his rule fostered cooperation between the Eritrean People’s Liberation Front (EPLF) and the Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF), which was waging a parallel campaign to overthrow the regime. Their common struggle contributed to Mengistu’s defeat in 1991, although the alliance concealed a fundamental difference between their political ambitions: the Eritrean movement sought to establish an independent state, while the Tigrayan movement aimed to overthrow the regime and restructure power within Ethiopia. A common enemy had united them, but victory exposed their conflicting visions of statehood. Eritrea gained independence in 1993 following a popular referendum endorsed by Ethiopia’s new government, then led by Meles Zenawi, and it was recognised by the international community. Independence made Ethiopia landlocked, losing its direct access to the Red Sea. Yet this did not disappear overnight. The country continued to use Assab under arrangements agreed with Eritrea, until mounting economic, territorial and political disputes culminated in the 1998–2000 war. This ended with the Algiers Agreement, followed by the boundary commission’s ruling in 2002. Relations between the two countries remained hostile and Ethiopia shifted almost all its maritime trade to Djibouti. Subsequent demographic and economic developments have sharpened the consequences. Ethiopia now has 135 million people, a growing industrial economy, and a thirst for international trade, but with almost all its foreign trade passing through Djibouti, it depends heavily on a single transit route. That dependence creates genuine economic vulnerabilities. Sign up for our Weekly Newsletter Get the best of Majalla, straight to your inbox. Ethiopia has 135 million people, a growing industrial base, and a thirst for international trade, but almost all trade depends on a single transit route through Djibouti 'Existential necessity' It is not surprising that a country of Ethiopia's size should want to diversify its maritime outlets and secure reliable access to global markets, but however legitimate its economic needs may be, they confer no sovereign entitlement to another country's territory. The right of access to the sea is fundamentally different from the right to a coastline, just as facilitating trade is distinct from redrawing borders. Since October 2023, Ethiopian Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed has increasingly presented access to the Red Sea as an existential necessity, bound up with the country's future and security. His rhetoric has extended beyond improving commercial transit arrangements to demands for sovereign maritime access and naval capabilities. He invoked history to portray the loss of Ethiopia's coastline as a historical wrong that now needed to be corrected. This rhetoric has coincided with severe domestic crises, particularly in the northern regions of Tigray, Amhara, and Oromia. In January 2024, Ethiopia signed a memorandum of understanding with local authorities in Somaliland, a coastal region of Somalia that wants to break away. The proposed arrangement envisaged a stretch of coastline and the establishment of a naval facility in exchange for Ethiopian recognition of Somaliland's independence. Somalia's federal government rejected the agreement as a violation of its sovereignty, triggering tensions. Mediation by Türkiye produced the Ankara Declaration in December 2024, which acknowledged the possibility of Ethiopia securing sustainable commercial access to the sea under Somali sovereignty, without granting it a sovereign coastal outlet. In December 2025, Israel (which also wants Red Sea access) became the first UN member state to recognise Somaliland. Ethiopia's attempt to obtain sovereign maritime access through the Somali coast stalled, which brought renewed attention to the port of Assab, which occupies a distinctive place in Ethiopia's political memory. Somaliland President Abdirahman Abdullahi Mohamed during a press conference with Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Sa'ar at the Presidential Palace in Hargeisa, 6 January 2026. Collapsing rapprochement The rapprochement between Ethiopia and Eritrea that began in 2018 was now collapsing. The reconciliation between Addis Ababa and Asmara had developed into a military alliance against the TPLF during the 2020-22 war, but the Pretoria Agreement, which ended that conflict, was subsequently signed without Eritrea's participation, creating a deep rift between the two countries. With no lasting framework for shared economic interests and mutual security guarantees, relations depended on a convergence of interests and calculations regarding domestic adversaries. As the arrangements underpinning Pretoria unravelled, Eritrea developed ties to the TPLF, despite them having fought so bitterly just a few years earlier. In September 2026, large-scale fighting resumed in Tigray. Ethiopian soldiers advanced, capturing Mekelle, the regional capital, before moving towards the Eritrean border. Thus began the latest and most dangerous phase. Addis Ababa and Asmara severed diplomatic relations and accused each other of military interference, support for armed groups, and aggression. Ethiopia invoked Article 51 of the UN Charter to justify measures it said it was taking in self-defence. Eritrea accused Ethiopia of using these claims as a pretext for seizing Assab. Military movements and mounting threats on both sides have now heightened the risk of war. This escalation cannot be understood in isolation. Foreign states have an interest in the Horn of Africa and seek to exploit state weaknesses. Ethiopia maintains close ties with the United Arab Emirates, which has economic and military influence in the ports of the region and across regional supply networks. Israel's recognition of Somaliland also signalled support for Ethiopia's ambitions to secure maritime access there. For Sudan, which has been ravaged by an ongoing civil war, the prospect of fighting between Ethiopia and Eritrea poses a direct threat. The Sudanese Armed Forces are fighting the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) militia, which now controls the giant Darfur region in western Sudan. The RSF supply network is said to include the UAE, but Abu Dhabi denies it. The International Crisis Group cites reports that RSF forces are stationed in the Benishangul-Gumuz region near the border and launch attacks from there into Sudan's Blue Nile region. Should war break out, the militarisation of the border, the flow of weapons and fighters, and further waves of displacement would compound these dangers, adding to the burden on Sudan. Any Ethiopia-Eritrea confrontation would therefore draw in overlapping conflicts and foreign actors. The harbour of Port Sudan on the Red Sea on 24 February 2014. It is Sudan's main seaport and source of 90% of its international trade. Dangers of escalation The maritime trade routes around the Horn of Africa are some of the world's busiest and most sensitive, as they intersect with the strategic interests of regional and global powers. Any extension of hostilities towards Eritrea's coastline would increase the risks to ports and shipping, drive up transport and insurance costs, and add more instability in a maritime corridor already suffering the repercussions of the civil war in Yemen. The African Union has a particular responsibility to turn its calls for restraint into urgent diplomatic action. It could reopen communication channels between Addis Ababa and Asmara, establish verifiable arrangements to prevent military clashes along the border, and support the resumption of a political process to address the conflict in Tigray. Regional governments could likewise approach the crisis as a shared threat to stability, rather than an opportunity to alter the balance of power in their favour. Saudi Arabia and Türkiye could help reduce tensions, forge understandings, and safeguard security in the Red Sea, but foreign powers supplying weapons must also commit to ending any military and financial assistance that fuels confrontation. Some call for peace while supplying the means to wage war. There is no inherent legal conflict between Ethiopia's right of access to the sea and Eritrea's sovereignty over its territory. International law recognises the legitimate interests and transit rights of landlocked states, while granting them no right to seize the territory of coastal countries. Respect for borders inherited at independence remains a cornerstone of the African regional order. Together with the prohibition on the use of force enshrined in the UN Charter, this principle places clear limits on territorial claims. A boatman transports visitors along a shore near the old port of Massawa—located 60 kilometers from the Eritrean capital—including civilians arriving from Ethiopia to visit Eritrea's Dahlak Islands. Contractual agreements, joint investments, and reciprocal security arrangements could provide practical solutions to the question of maritime access without reopening disputes over sovereignty. Ethiopia and Eritrea have already demonstrated that Eritrean independence can coexist with Ethiopian use of the port of Assab. Geography did not end that arrangement; it collapsed because political and security understandings between the two countries broke down. Renewing cooperation will require more than another port agreement; it will demand measures to address mutual security concerns, backed by international guarantees. A region at stake Assab represents a test of the future political and security order in the Horn of Africa, with implications far beyond the fate of a port. Ethiopia's need for maritime access is an economic and strategic reality, but turning that need into a claim to sovereignty is no remedy for the underlying economic problem and threatens to ignite a fresh dispute over borders and legitimacy. For Eritrea, defending independence and sovereignty is compatible with establishing good economic relations with its larger neighbour. For the countries of the Horn of Africa, not least Sudan, preventing war is essential to protecting their own security and sovereignty. ethiopia.summary: The port of Assab has become a focal point in the escalating tensions between Ethiopia and Eritrea, with Ethiopia asserting that access to the Red Sea is an "existential" issue. The historical context of the dispute dates back to colonial times, with Assab symbolizing Ethiopia's loss of direct maritime access following Eritrea's independence in 1993. Ethiopia's population and economy have grown significantly, increasing its need for diversified trade routes beyond its reliance on Djibouti. Recent developments, including Ethiopia's military buildup near the Eritrean border and the breakdown of diplomatic relations, have heightened fears of conflict. Ethiopia's Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed has framed the issue as a historical grievance, while Eritrea views Assab as integral to its sovereignty. The situation is further complicated by regional dynamics, including foreign interests from countries like the UAE and Israel. The potential for war poses risks not only to the two nations but also to regional stability, particularly affecting Sudan amidst its ongoing civil conflict.

ethiopia.content: Ethiopia Takes Delivery of 12 Su-35 Fighter Jets, to Receive S-400 Air Defense Systems: PM Abiy - ENA English - ENA Skip to Content Ethiopia Takes Delivery of 12 Su-35 Fighter Jets, to Receive S-400 Air Defense Systems: PM Abiy - ENA English Live: አማርኛ ትግርኛ Afaan Oromoo Af‑Soomaali Qafar Afa English Français عربي Politics Social Economy Sport Technology Environment Feature Videos About Us Ethiopia Takes Delivery of 12 Su-35 Fighter Jets, to Receive S-400 Air Defense Systems: PM Abiy 🔇Unmute Addis Ababa, October 28, 2026 (ENA)— Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed has announced that the country has taken delivery of its first 12 Su-35 4++ generation fighter jets and is set to receive four batteries of S-400 air defense systems. The Prime Minister described the move as a significant milestone in Ethiopia’s efforts to strengthen its national defense and security capabilities. In a social media post, PM Abiy said Ethiopia’s comprehensive efforts to sustainably ensure peace and security had reached a new milestone. He added that the growing readiness of the country’s defense forces was enhancing its ability to deter potential aggression. “Today, in accordance with our prior agreement with the Russian government, we have taken delivery of the first twelve Su-35 4++ Generation fighter jets,” he said, adding that Ethiopia would also receive four S-400 air defense system batteries. Prime Minister Abiy expressed gratitude to Russian President Vladimir Putin for facilitating the delivery of the fighter jets a year ahead of the agreed schedule. He said the acquisition places Ethiopia at the forefront of Sub-Saharan African nations in equipping itself with the advanced fighter jets. The Prime Minister further elaborated that the development further strengthens Ethiopia’s sovereignty and enhances its defense capabilities, enabling the country to pursue its national security objectives while contributing to regional stability. The announcement comes as Prime Minister Abiy arrives in Moscow, Russia, to attend the Third Russia–Africa Summit, providing an opportunity to advance Ethiopia’s engagement with Russia and other African nations. The Prime Minister described the acquisition as a significant boost to Ethiopia’s collective security and its long-term efforts to safeguard national sovereignty and regional peace. © Ethiopian News Agency 2023 Hidden

ENDF and TPLF Battle Across Tigray Source: Michael DeAngelo, Liam Karr, and Alexander Brown Eastern Axis: Afar Region Nothing significant to report. Northern Axis: Rama-Zalambessa-Dallol The Ethiopian military (Ethiopian National Defense Force, ENDF) has conducted consecutive days of drone strikes in TPLF-held Rama, a town on the Eritrean border, amid reported fighting around the Rama-Adwa highway. The Tigray Defense Forces (TDF), the TPLF’s military wing, retook Rama on October 22 following an ENDF withdrawal from the town. [i] Several conflict trackers on social media have reported ENDF drone strikes in Rama the past few days, with the analyst and mapper The Ethiopian Conflict Map stating that the strikes began on October 27. [ii] The ENDF conducted a drone strike on October 30 that killed at least 12 civilians, who were reportedly collecting grain from a transport truck that had been struck the previous day. [iii] The Ethiopian Conflict Map and a pro-Fano account on X have reported fighting between the ENDF and TDF on both sides of highway that connects Rama to ENDF-held Adwa, which is approximately 20 miles to the south, since October 28. [iv] Western Axis: Humera-Addi Remets-Shire The ENDF and TDF continued clashing northwest of Shire as the ENDF attempts to consolidate control of the area. The two sides clashed near Adi Nebreid and Adi Hageray, which is 40 miles northwest of Shire, on October 27 and 28 after the ENDF reportedly advanced into the area. [v] Fighting reportedly occurred north of the two towns, which are on a road that connects Sheraro approximately 20 miles to the west. Pro-TPLF journalist Yonas Nigussie and a pro-Fano account on X separately reported that the TDF repelled the ENDF. [vi] Central Axis: Abiy Addi-Adwa-Axum Ethiopian federal forces and the TDF have continued fighting over control of the mountainous Tigray interior. Federal forces have continued efforts to clear the TDF from its mountain havens around Abiy Addi, which is 55 miles west of Mekele, after capturing both Abiy Addi and Zana on October 22. [vii] Armed Conflict Location & Event Data (ACLED) and The Ethiopian Conflict Map reported that federal forces gained control of multiple areas around Kola Tembien, which is just northwest of Abiy Addi, amid clashes with the TDF from October 27 to 29. [viii] Federal forces have also attempted to clear the TDF from havens near Tigray’s city belt, specifically on both sides of Tigray’s main east-west highway. Federal forces have repeatedly clashed with the TDF around the highway since October 20. [ix] ACLED reported federal movements toward Werie Lehe, which is approximately 40 miles southeast of Adwa, from positions to the south and west on October 28. [x] The Ethiopian Conflict Map reported fighting between federal forces and the TDF in the area on the same day. [xi] Clashes also reportedly occurred near Chila, which is between Axum and Shire approximately 15 miles north of the east-west highway, on October 28 and 29 amid reported federal artillery strikes. [xii] Southern Axis: Mekele-Alamata-Sekota-Woldia Nothing significant to report. Northern Amhara Sector: From B22 Highway Northward The ENDF reportedly conducted drone strikes targeting the Amhara Fano National Movement in mountainous areas around the A2 highway between Dessie and Woldia. The Ethiopian Conflict Map and two pro-Fano sources reported on October 29 that the ENDF conducted strikes near Hayk, which is 20 miles north of Dessie. [xiii] The pro-Fano sources alleged that the strikes hit an internally displaced persons camp, killing over a dozen civilians. [xiv] Other Rebel Kinetic Activity The Oromo Liberation Army (OLA) reportedly clashed with federal and regional forces in western Oromia region. Multiple news outlets had previously reported on October 20 and 21 that suspected OLA militants attacked a sugar factory in Fincha, which is in the Horo Guduru Welega zone approximately 175 miles northwest of Addis Ababa, the Ethiopian capital. [xv] The attack, which would have been one of the OLA’s first since the war between the federal government and Alliance for Survival rebel coalition began in September 2026, reportedly killed several security officers and elicited a federal drone strike against the militants. [xvi] The Ethiopian Conflict Map reported on October 29 that the OLA clashed again with federal police and Oromia regional forces in Fincha. [xvii] Major Domestic Political Developments AFNM figure Eskinder Nega announced that he was leaving the AFNM. Eskinder had led the Amhara Fano Peace Organization, one of the groups that merged to form the AFNM, and voiced support for AFNM’s creation in January 2026, despite reportedly declining to serve as its policy and strategy head. [xviii] Deutsche Welle reported on October 28 that Eskinder stated that he was leaving the AFNM due to the group’s membership in the Alliance for Survival, specifically citing the TPLF’s influence in the coalition. [xix] Regional and International Activity Ethiopia and Russia reaffirmed their intent to strengthen ties at the Russia-Africa Summit, with Russia delivering fighter jets to Ethiopia amid the summit. Ethiopian Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed and Russian President Vladimir Putin met on October 28 on the sidelines of the summit in Moscow and expressed their mutual interest in deepening cooperation between the two countries. [xx] Abiy emphasized nuclear energy cooperation as a priority, calling for increased funding and training for Ethiopian experts. [xxi] The Russian ambassador to Ethiopia said in an interview with Russian state media published on October 26 that Russia and Ethiopia are drafting an agreement to cooperate on the construction of a nuclear power plant in Ethiopia, with Abiy reporting progress on the agreement on October 29. [xxii] Russia delivered fighter jets to Ethiopia amid the summit as part of a preexisting deal. Abiy thanked Putin on X on October 28 for the delivery of Russian Su-35 fighter jets, which Abiy said Russia delivered a year ahead of schedule. [xxiii] Abiy stated that Russia would deliver 12 fighter jets, although the Russian state-owned arms exporter Rosoboronexport commented to Reuters that it had delivered two fighter jets to the Ethiopian Air Force. [xxiv] The prime minister also said that Russia will eventually deliver four S-400 surface-to-air missile batteries. [xxv] Abiy portrayed the delivery as part of Ethiopian efforts to “preemptively deter aggression.” [xxvi] Eritrean Minister of Information Yemane Gebremeskel stated on X on October 28 that the delivery will support an Ethiopian “‘pre-emptive’ war of aggression.” [xxvii] Ethiopia welcomed the candidacy of Emirati diplomat Lana Nusseibeh for United Nations-Secretary General. Nusseibeh previously announced her candidacy on October 22. [xxviii] The Ethiopian Ministry of Foreign Affairs said on X on October 29 that Ethiopia “welcomes” Nusseibeh’s candidacy, pointing to her diplomatic experience. [xxix] Nusseibeh expressed gratitude to the Ethiopian foreign ministry on October 30. [xxx] The Ethiopian Navy held a four-day forum on security in the Red Sea and conjoining waterways including naval officers from Djibouti, Oman, Puntland, Somaliland, and Yemen. The Ethiopian Navy hosted the forum, which was sponsored by the European Union, at its headquarters from October 26 to 29. [xxxi] The forum was intended to increase maritime cooperation among the participants in search-and-rescue operations and broader security matters.
