The warning, issued on October 30, comes as El Niño-related rainfall creates favourable conditions for the spread of the mosquito-borne virus across Eastern Africa. FAO's October assessment identified newly suitable areas for transmission in southern Somalia and forecast a further expansion of favourable conditions across the region through January 2027. The assessment does not confirm an outbreak in Somalia. Instead, it signals an increased risk that authorities must prepare for before infections emerge or spread. The threat carries economic implications for communities that depend on livestock for their livelihoods. Rift Valley fever can cause severe illness in animals and humans, while livestock deaths and pregnancy losses can inflict significant financial damage on affected households. According to the World Health Organization (WHO), the disease can cause serious illness in livestock, threatening the animals on which many rural livelihoods depend. For livestock owners, the potential losses extend beyond animals that die from infection. Pregnancy losses can also undermine the productive capacity of affected herds, increasing the economic burden of the disease. Rainfall Raises Transmission Risk Heavy rainfall is a central factor behind the latest warning. Wet conditions can expand mosquito breeding grounds, increasing the potential for transmission. Movements of livestock can also contribute to the spread of infection, making surveillance and coordination between neighbouring countries important. The FAO assessment indicates that environmental conditions suitable for transmission have emerged in additional areas of southern Somalia. It also forecasts that conditions favourable to the disease could expand across Eastern Africa through January 2027, extending the period during which authorities may need to maintain heightened surveillance. The warning places Somalia within a broader regional risk picture rather than identifying a confirmed national outbreak. Agencies Call for Early Action FAO and IGAD urged countries facing elevated risk to strengthen targeted surveillance, position vaccines and essential supplies in advance, and coordinate animal-health and public-health responses across borders. The recommended measures are intended to improve preparedness before outbreaks place additional pressure on livestock owners and health services. Cross-border coordination is particularly important because livestock movements can contribute to disease transmission, while rainfall-driven mosquito breeding conditions may affect multiple countries. The agencies' recommendations focus on detecting potential infections and ensuring that essential resources are available when needed. advertisements Human Health and Livestock Losses Rift Valley fever poses a dual threat to animal production and human health. The WHO says most human infections occur through contact with the blood or organs of infected animals. People can also become infected through bites from mosquitoes carrying the virus. No human-to-human transmission has been documented, according to the WHO. The disease's impact on animals is a major economic concern. Livestock deaths and pregnancy losses can reduce the productive value of affected herds and threaten the livelihoods of households that rely on them. Somalia has experienced Rift Valley fever during earlier periods of exceptional rainfall. The WHO records a major outbreak in 1997–98 that affected Somalia, Kenya and Tanzania following an El Niño event accompanied by extensive flooding. That history provides a precedent for the current concern, although the latest assessment identifies transmission risk rather than confirmed infections. For Somalia, the immediate priority is preparedness. The effectiveness of targeted surveillance, advance positioning of vaccines and supplies, and coordination with neighbouring countries will be critical as rainfall-related transmission conditions are forecast to persist through January 2027. Facebook Instagram X VKontakte Youtube Somali Guardian News Somalia Africa World Featured Editor Picks Editorials Home News Somalia UN mission in Somalia closes after three decades UN mission in Somalia closes after three decades October 31, 2026 Share Facebook X Pinterest WhatsApp MOGADISHU (Somaliguardian) – The United Nations Transitional Assistance Mission in Somalia (UNTMIS) ceased operations on Saturday, ending more than three decades of UN missions in the country at the Somali government’s request. The closure completes a two-year transition under Security Council resolutions 2753 (2024) and 2809 (2025), the United Nations said in a statement from the spokesperson for Secretary-General Antonio Guterres, Stéphane Dujarric, dated Oct 26. Under a roadmap agreed with the Federal Government of Somalia, UNTMIS’s mandated functions have been transferred to Somali institutions and to UN agencies, funds and programmes. The statement said Guterres commends “the determination and resilience of the Somali people” and acknowledges significant political, security, humanitarian and development challenges that remain. It urged sustained international support for inclusive political dialogue, reconciliation, stronger institutions and human rights. It also stressed the need for continued backing in addressing the threat from Al Shabaab and enabling a gradual, sustainable security transition. The UN will keep working in Somalia through its resident agencies, funds and programmes, in partnership with Somali authorities, the African Union and other international partners, the statement said. “The closure of UNTMIS does not signal the end of UN support,” said Raisedon Zenenga, the mission’s officer-in-charge, describing it as the opening of a new chapter in the partnership. A farewell ceremony was held in Mogadishu on Oct 26, led by Zenenga and Deputy Prime Minister Salah Ahmed Jama. Jama hailed the closure as a “day of victory”, according to media reports. BACKGROUND UNTMIS was established by Security Council resolution 2753, adopted on Oct 30, 2024, and began operations on Nov 1, 2024, succeeding the UN Assistance Mission in Somalia (UNSOM), which had operated since June 2013. UN missions in Somalia date back to 1992, through the UNOSOM operations and the UN Political Office for Somalia (UNPOS) from 1995. The closure comes amid a sharp decline in funding for Somalia, which the Secretary-General has flagged as a concern, and after years of sometimes strained relations between Somali governments and the mission, whose role in domestic politics has at times prompted accusations of interference. It does not affect the separate African Union Support and Stabilisation Mission in Somalia (AUSSOM), whose mandate expires on Dec 31 unless extended. AU troops rely on the UN Support Office in Somalia (UNSOS) for food, fuel, medical care and transport, and Reuters reported in September that a U.S.-backed plan could end that support by December 2027. After 20 years of a lot of blood and sacrifice we are handing over security to our Somali brothers,” Gen. Muhoozi Kainerugaba, chief of Uganda’s defense forces, wrote on X. advertisements Ugandan authorities have not publicly announced how many troops are leaving, which bases will be handed over first or when the withdrawal will be completed. Uganda remains the largest troop contributor to the African Union Support and Stabilization Mission in Somalia, or AUSSOM. The African Union authorized 4,500 Ugandan troops for the mission, which replaced the African Union Transition Mission in Somalia at the start of 2025. AUSSOM’s mandate includes supporting Somali forces against al-Shabab, protecting civilians and key infrastructure, and gradually transferring security responsibilities to Somali security institutions. The mission’s current transition plan envisages a phased drawdown toward a final exit by December 2029, subject to security conditions. Uganda first deployed troops to Somalia in March 2007 as the lead contingent in the African Union Mission in Somalia, or AMISOM, becoming one of the longest-serving foreign military contributors to the country’s security operations. Ugandan forces have since fought in some of the most significant battles against al-Shabab and have operated across Mogadishu and large parts of Lower Shabelle. The deployment has also come at a heavy cost. Ugandan troops have suffered repeated casualties in al-Shabab attacks, including major assaults on African Union bases over the course of the mission. The announcement comes as AUSSOM faces persistent funding shortages. The African Union Peace and Security Council has repeatedly warned that inadequate and unpredictable financing threatens the mission’s operations and has called for additional international support. The AU has also emphasized that decisions over AUSSOM’s future and troop withdrawals should be based on assessments of conditions on the ground and coordinated with Somalia to avoid creating security gaps. Uganda has remained a central part of that security architecture. Earlier this year, the African Union praised Kampala for deploying additional troops to Somalia on a bilateral basis as a temporary response to deteriorating security conditions. Al-Shabab, an al-Qaeda-linked militant group, continues to control or operate across parts of rural southern and central Somalia despite nearly two decades of military pressure from Somali forces and their international partners. Kainerugaba’s announcement therefore represents a significant shift in Uganda’s long-running role in Somalia, but it remains unclear whether the move marks the beginning of a full national withdrawal or a phased reduction coordinated with AUSSOM and Somali authorities. Dowladda Federaalka Galmudug Hiiraan News Jubaland News Koonfur Galbeed SSC Somaliland Follow us Search News Somalia UN political mission in Somalia closes after decades of support Posted by: Horseed Staff The United Nations is ending its political mission in Somalia, bringing to a close a chapter of international engagement that has accompanied the country through decades of conflict, political change and efforts to rebuild state institutions. 31 October, 2026 Share Tweet UN Somalia/Adihamiid Mohamed Raisedon Zenenga, Officer-in-Charge of UNTMIS, delivers remarks at a ceremony marking the closure of the mission. The UN Transitional Assistance Mission in Somalia (UNTMIS) formally wraps up its work on Saturday, with the organisation saying responsibility for the country’s recovery will increasingly rest with Somali institutions. UN Deputy Special Representative James Swan said the mission’s closure came after “considerable progress” in Somalia, while acknowledging that significant challenges remained. “Somalia today possesses national and federal institutions that did not exist when the UN’s political engagement began,” said UN Deputy Special Representative Adam Abdelmoula Zenenga. He pointed to progress in state formation, political inclusion, constitutional processes, human rights frameworks and the development of governance structures that allow for Somali-led decision-making. However, Mr Zenenga said continued international engagement would remain important to sustaining those gains and addressing unresolved priorities. From civil war to state-building Somalia has undergone profound change since the early 1990s, when the collapse of central government institutions and the outbreak of civil war plunged the country into prolonged conflict and instability. The crisis triggered a major movement of refugees and internally displaced people. Insecurity, disputed electoral processes and constitutional reform efforts have added to the difficulties, while repeated droughts and floods have compounded humanitarian needs. Successive UN political missions have supported Somalia through key stages of its peacebuilding and state-building efforts, including attempts to restore governance, rebuild institutions and promote national reconciliation. With UNTMIS now closing, those responsibilities will increasingly be carried by Somali institutions, alongside continued support from UN agencies operating in the country. UN agencies continue humanitarian work The closure of UNTMIS does not mark the end of the UN’s presence in Somalia. About 25 UN entities continue to operate across the country, providing humanitarian and development assistance. In September, the UN migration agency, IOM, helped rehabilitate a vegetable market in the town of Balcad. The renovated market has 56 stalls, running water and solar lighting, with about 70% of the stalls allocated to women-headed households, women-led businesses and small enterprises. Somalia’s health ministry, working with Unicef, has also introduced national guidelines for the care of newborn babies, including those who are premature, small or sick. In Puntland, the UN food agency FAO is supporting a school meals programme connecting 1,330 local farmers and fisherfolk with schools serving about 18,700 children. Meanwhile, in Baidoa, UN mine-action specialists have worked with Somali authorities to teach hundreds of students and teachers how to identify the dangers posed by explosive remnants of war. Humanitarian needs remain severe Despite progress in state-building, Somalia continues to face a complex humanitarian crisis. The UN’s humanitarian affairs office, OCHA, says conflict and climate-related shocks continue to reinforce each other. Families displaced by drought or violence can face further displacement as a result of flooding or renewed fighting. An estimated 4.8 million people in Somalia — out of a population of just under 20 million — require humanitarian assistance this year. Aid organisations have appealed for $852m to provide assistance to 2.4 million people. By mid-October, about 35% of the requested funding had been received. The UN has also called for continued international support to counter the threat posed by the militant group al-Shabab and to help Somalia move towards a gradual and sustainable security transition. Poverty and economic pressures For Somalia’s leaders, tackling poverty is likely to remain a major challenge as the country moves beyond the UN political mission. The economy remains fragile and heavily dependent on subsistence farming, livestock, pastoralism and money sent home by Somalis living abroad. The country also relies heavily on imports, with more than 90% of essential goods coming from overseas, according to OCHA. The combination of poverty, insecurity, climate shocks and limited economic opportunities presents a continuing challenge to the country’s long-term recovery. ‘A new chapter’ The closure of UNTMIS marks a change in the nature of the UN’s engagement with Somalia rather than a complete withdrawal. Humanitarian and development agencies will continue to operate in the country, supporting government institutions and communities. “Today is not an end to the partnership between the United Nations and Somalia,” Mr Zenenga said. “It marks the conclusion of one chapter and the beginning of another.” Explore more on these topics Mogadishu Somalia UN Related Posts Uganda Begins Troop Withdrawal from Somalia After Nearly 20 Years 2 min read Puntland President Calls on Somalia’s President to Resign 1 min read Somalia: Armed Group Reportedly Hijacks Iranian Fishing Vessel off Puntland Coast 1 min read Somalia says it will not take sides in Ethiopia-Eritrea tensions 1 min read Back to top Horseed Media About Profile Contact us Privacy Policy Terms and Conditions Category Wararka Soomaaliya Puntland News News Somalia Dowladda Federaalka World News ©2026 Horseed Media Ltd
somalia.summary: The United Nations has officially closed its political mission in Somalia, concluding decades of support that began during a period of civil war and state collapse in the early 1990s. The UN Transitional Assistance Mission in Somalia (UNTMIS) ended its operations, with officials noting significant progress in establishing national and federal institutions, despite ongoing challenges. UN Deputy Special Representative Adam Abdelmoula Zenenga highlighted advancements in governance, political inclusion, and human rights frameworks. However, he emphasized the need for continued international support to sustain these gains. While the mission's closure transfers responsibilities to Somali institutions, approximately 25 UN agencies will remain active in the country, providing humanitarian and development assistance. Somalia continues to face a severe humanitarian crisis, with 4.8 million people requiring aid, exacerbated by conflict and climate-related shocks. The UN's departure marks a transition rather than a complete withdrawal, as it aims to support Somalia's ongoing recovery and development efforts.

Dowladda Federaalka Galmudug Hiiraan News Jubaland News Koonfur Galbeed SSC Somaliland Follow us Search News Somalia Uganda Begins Troop Withdrawal from Somalia After Nearly 20 Years Posted by: Horseed Staff Uganda has begun withdrawing troops from Somalia after nearly two decades of military deployments, the country’s army chief has announced, marking the start of a security handover to Somali forces. 31 October, 2026 Share Tweet Gen Muhoozi Kainerugaba, Uganda’s Chief of Defence Forces, said on Thursday that Ugandan troops had started leaving Somalia. “As we promised, we have started withdrawing UPDF from Somalia. After 20 years of a lot of blood and sacrifice we are handing over security to our Somali brothers,” he wrote on X. Ugandan authorities have not said how many troops are being withdrawn, which bases will be handed over first or when the process is expected to be completed. Uganda is the largest troop contributor to the African Union Support and Stabilization Mission in Somalia (AUSSOM). The African Union has authorised 4,500 Ugandan troops for the mission, which replaced the African Union Transition Mission in Somalia (ATMIS) at the beginning of 2025. AUSSOM supports Somali forces in operations against al-Shabab, protects civilians and key infrastructure, and assists with the gradual transfer of security responsibilities to Somalia’s security institutions. Under the current transition plan, the mission is expected to reduce its presence in phases, with a final withdrawal envisaged by December 2029, subject to security conditions. Long-running military presence Uganda first deployed troops to Somalia in March 2007 as the lead contingent of the African Union Mission in Somalia (AMISOM). Since then, Ugandan forces have taken part in some of the most significant military operations against al-Shabab and have operated in Mogadishu and large parts of Lower Shabelle. The deployment has come at a significant human cost. Ugandan troops have suffered repeated casualties in attacks by al-Shabab, including major assaults on African Union military bases. The announcement comes as AUSSOM faces continuing financial challenges. The African Union Peace and Security Council has repeatedly warned that inadequate and unpredictable funding threatens the mission’s ability to operate effectively and has called for greater international support. The African Union has also stressed that decisions on the mission’s future and the withdrawal of troops should be based on security conditions on the ground and coordinated with the Somali government to prevent gaps in security. Uganda has remained a key part of Somalia’s security arrangements. Earlier this year, the African Union praised Kampala for deploying additional troops to Somalia on a bilateral basis as a temporary response to deteriorating security conditions. Uncertain next phase Al-Shabab, an al-Qaeda-linked militant group, continues to operate and maintain control over parts of rural southern and central Somalia, despite nearly two decades of military operations by Somali forces and their international partners. Gen Kainerugaba’s announcement represents a significant change in Uganda’s long-standing military role in Somalia. However, it remains unclear whether the move signals a complete Ugandan withdrawal or the beginning of a phased reduction coordinated with AUSSOM and Somali authorities. السوداني الأول، والاتحاد السوداني لكرة القدم نحو منعطف بالغ الخطورة، في ظل تصاعد الضغوط والتدخلات التي باتت تحاصر المدرب، وتضع تجربته مع صقور الجديان على المحك، وسط مؤشرات متزايدة على اقتراب نهاية مشواره مع المنتخب. وتشير المعلومات التي تحصل عليها “الترا سودان” من داخل مجلس إدارة الاتحاد إلى أن أبياه بات يشعر بأن ما يتعرض له يمثل تحركات منظمة تستهدف تقويض صلاحياته وإضعاف موقفه، تمهيداً لإبعاده عن قيادة المنتخب. وهو ما أسرّ به لعدد من المقربين منه، معبّراً عن استيائه الشديد من الأجواء التي يعمل فيها. وبحسب المعلومات ذاتها، فإن المدرب الغاني بات يعتقد أن هناك مخططاً يُحاك ضده، وأن بعض القرارات والتوجهات الأخيرة داخل الاتحاد لا يمكن فصلها عن مساعٍ لإجباره على مغادرة موقعه، بعدما وجد نفسه في مواجهة تدخلات متكررة في صميم اختصاصاته الفنية. التغييرات التي طالت الجهازين الإداري والفني المساعد لم تكن أمراً عابراً بالنسبة للمدرب الغاني، خصوصاً بعد إبعاد المدير الإداري أبوبكر الماحي، وابتعاد المدرب العام صلاح الفنج عن موقعه ضمن المنظومة التي عملت معه خلال الفترة الماضية. ويمثل الرجلان عنصرين مهمين في منظومة أبياه، وكان المدرب ينظر إليهما باعتبارهما من ركائز الاستقرار داخل المنتخب، الأمر الذي دفعه إلى المطالبة بإعادة ترتيب الأوضاع بما يضمن عودة الانسجام إلى الجهازين الفني والإداري. لكن ما حدث عزز شعوره بأن هناك توجهاً لإعادة تشكيل المنظومة المحيطة به، دون اعتبار لرؤيته أو احتياجاته، وبكوادر لا تمتلك بالضرورة الخبرة المطلوبة للعمل في منتخب بحجم صقور الجديان. ومن أكثر الملفات التي أثارت غضب أبياه الضغوط المتواصلة بشأن إبعاد عدد من أصحاب الخبرة والعناصر الأساسية التي شكلت العمود الفقري للمنتخب خلال مشواره الأخير. فالمدرب الغاني لا يرى مبرراً للتخلي عن عناصر أثبتت جدارتها وقدمت الكثير للمنتخب، لمجرد ارتباط بعضها بملف المطالبة بالمستحقات المالية. كما لا يخفي تحفظاته على محاولات فرض أسماء جديدة ضمن القائمة، دون أن تكون هناك قناعة فنية مكتملة بشأن قدراتها. وتفاقمت الأزمة مع التوجه نحو تغيير نسبة من قوام المنتخب وإقحام عناصر من منتخب الشباب، في وقت يرى فيه أبياه أن الإحلال والتجديد لا ينبغي أن يتحولا إلى قرارات فوقية تتجاوز التقييم الفني واحتياجات المنتخب. ولم تتوقف مصادر الإحباط عند التدخل في اختيار اللاعبين وإدارة الجهاز الفني، بل امتدت إلى عدم تنفيذ عدد من البرامج الإعدادية التي اقترحها المدرب، وفي مقدمتها إقامة معسكر مبكر عقب فراغ الهلال والمريخ من مشاركتهما في البطولات الأفريقية. وكان أبياه يعوّل على الاستفادة من تلك الفترة في تجهيز المنتخب بصورة مثالية، والاستفادة من وجود العناصر الأساسية في السودان. غير أن عدم الاستجابة للمقترح أضاف حلقة جديدة إلى سلسلة الخلافات بينه والاتحاد. وبدا للمدرب أن برامجه وتصوراته لا تجد الاهتمام المطلوب، وأنه مطالب بتحقيق النتائج وتحمل المسؤولية كاملة، دون أن تتوفر له الظروف والصلاحيات اللازمة. التطور الأكثر إثارة في هذه الأزمة أن أبياه، وفقاً للمعلومات التي تحصلت عليها مصادرنا، لمح للمقربين منه بأن مواجهتي المنتخب أمام السنغال ذهاباً وإياباً قد تكونان آخر مشاويره مع صقور الجديان. وتشير هذه المعطيات إلى أن المدرب الغاني بدأ بالفعل التفكير في وضع حد لتجربته عقب المباراتين، في ظل قناعته بأن الأجواء الحالية لم تعد تساعده على مواصلة العمل بالصورة التي يريدها، وأن حجم التدخلات والضغوط تجاوز الحدود التي يمكن التعايش معها. وإذا مضى أبياه في هذا الاتجاه، فإن المنتخب الوطني سيكون أمام خسارة مدرب كبير قاده إلى مرحلة مميزة من النتائج والإنجازات، في وقت يحتاج فيه إلى الاستقرار والاستمرارية أكثر من حاجته إلى الدخول في مغامرة فنية وإدارية جديدة. ما يحدث الآن يتجاوز خلافاً حول قائمة أو لاعب أو معسكر إعدادي. نحن أمام أزمة ثقة تتسع يوماً بعد يوم، ومدرب بات يشعر بأنه مستهدف، وأن هناك من يعمل على إضعاف تجربته وإفقاده أدوات النجاح، قبل أن يصبح رحيله أمراً واقعاً. والسؤال الذي ينبغي أن يجيب عنه الاتحاد السوداني لكرة القدم ليس ما إذا كان أبياه سيغادر فحسب، بل من يتحمل مسؤولية الوصول بعلاقة المنتخب مع مدرب صنع معه إنجازات كبيرة إلى هذه المرحلة؟ هل هناك مشروع فني بديل يستحق التضحية بتجربة أبياه؟ أم أن صقور الجديان يدفعون ثمن صراعات وتدخلات إدارية لا علاقة لها بمصلحة المنتخب؟ المؤكد أن خسارة أبياه، إن حدثت بالطريقة التي تلوح في الأفق، ستكون بداية هدم مشروع كان يستحق الحماية والاستقرار والبناء عليه. اتحاد كرة القدم صقور الجديان كواسي أبياه 102 مشاركة أخبار ذات صلة رياضة أبياه يعلن القائمة الأولية لصقور football.summary: كشف الاتحاد الأفريقي لكرة القدم «كاف» عن مواعيد مباريات الأندية المصرية الزمالك وبيراميدز والأهلي في بطولتي دوري أبطال أفريقيا والكونفدرالية لموسم 2026/2027. حيث سيتنافس الزمالك وبيراميدز في دوري أبطال أفريقيا، بينما يشارك الأهلي في الكونفدرالية. تم تقسيم الفرق إلى أربع مجموعات، حيث وقع الزمالك في المجموعة الثانية مع يانج أفريكانز التنزاني، مولودية الجزائر، والنادي الأفريقي التونسي. تبدأ مباريات الزمالك في الجولة الأولى بمواجهة الأفريقي التونسي في نهاية نوفمبر 2026. من جهة أخرى، يلعب بيراميدز في المجموعة الرابعة مع الهلال السوداني، حوريا الغيني، والمغرب الفاسي، حيث يواجه المغرب الفاسي في الجولة الأولى. أما الأهلي، فقد وقع في المجموعة الأولى مع الرجاء المغربي، أول أغسطس الأنجولي، وإسكو كارا التوجولي، حيث يبدأ مبارياته بمواجهة أول أغسطس. ستنطلق المنافسات في نوفمبر 2026.
